title: I buy, I go, I see
goal: Use second-conjugation verbs and the eleven irregular verbs in the present tense.
bekal: build the second-conjugation present: *ceannaím, ceannaíonn tú, ceannaímid*
spot verbs that drop a letter in the middle: *oscail* → *osclaím*
use the eleven most common irregular verbs

dialogs.title: Comhrá — An deireadh seachtaine
dialogs.intro: Seán asks Budi what he usually does at the weekend.

lines.speaker: Seán:
lines.text: Cá dtéann tú ag an deireadh seachtaine?
lines.id: Where do you usually go at the weekend?
lines.literal: where go you at the end week-of?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Téim go dtí an chathair. Ceannaím bia sa mhargadh.
lines.id: I go into town. I buy food at the market.
lines.literal: go-I to the city. buy-I food in-the market.

lines.speaker: Seán:
lines.id: Do your friends come with you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tagann, uaireanta. Tosaímid ar a deich.
lines.literal: come, sometimes. start-we on the ten.

lines.speaker: Seán:
lines.id: And what do you do then?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Féachaimid ar na siopaí. Uaireanta faighimid caife.
lines.id: We look around the shops. Sometimes we get coffee.
lines.literal: look-we on the shops. sometimes get-we coffee.

lines.speaker: Seán:
lines.id: Do you see the street musicians?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Feicim iad gach Satharn. Tugaim euro dóibh.
lines.id: I see them every Saturday. I give them a euro.
lines.literal: see-I them every Saturday. give-I euro to-them.

lines.speaker: Seán:
lines.text: Deas! An imíonn tú go luath?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Imím ar a cúig. Críochnaím an lá le dinnéar.
lines.id: I leave at five. I finish the day with dinner.
lines.literal: leave-I on the five. finish-I the day with dinner.

lines.speaker: Seán:
lines.text: An gcabhraíonn tú le Mam sa chistin?
lines.id: Do you help Mam in the kitchen?
lines.literal: question help you with Mam in-the kitchen?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Cabhraím go minic — ach ní ullmhaím an dinnéar!
lines.id: Often — but I don't make the dinner!
lines.literal: help-I often — but not prepare-I the dinner!

notes: **Second conjugation: long endings.** Where the first conjugation uses *-aim / -ann*, the second uses *-aím / -aíonn*. Only one fada separates them, but the sound is clearly different: *ólaim* (OH-lim) versus *ceannaím* (KYAH-neem). How to spot them: second-conjugation verbs have **two or more syllables** and almost always end in *-igh* — *ceannaigh*, *tosaigh*, *críochnaigh*, *imigh*, *cabhraigh*, *ullmhaigh*.

**Oscail → osclaím: a letter drops out.** A group of second-conjugation verbs ending in *-il, -in, -ir, -is* lose the vowel in the middle as soon as an ending is added: *oscail* → *osclaím*, *inis* → *insím*, *freagair* → *freagraím*, *imir* → *imrím*, *codail* → *codlaím*, *labhair* → *labhraím*. This is called syncopation, and it happens because Irish avoids three weak syllables in a row.

**Faighimid, feicim, tugaim, tagaim, téim — forms you can't guess.** Irish has eleven irregular verbs, and unluckily they are the eleven used most. The good news: in the present tense most of them behave normally once you know the stem — *faigh* → *faighim*, *feic* → *feicim*, *tabhair* → *tugaim*, *tar* → *tagaim*, *téigh* → *téim*. The really dramatic changes only come in the past tense (Unit 17).

**Cá dtéann tú? — cá brings urú, just like an.** You saw it in *Cá bhfuil …?* in Unit 3. Now the pattern is complete: *cá* and *an* both bring urú to the verb after them, while *ní* brings séimhiú. Three little words, three behaviors, and all three will keep showing up in every remaining unit.

blocks.title: How to tell the first and second conjugations apart
items: **One syllable → first conjugation.** *Ól, fan, glan, dún, cuir, bris, tuig, rith, léigh.*
**Two syllables ending in -igh → second conjugation.** *Ceannaigh, tosaigh, éirigh, imigh, cabhraigh.*
**Two syllables ending in -il, -in, -ir, -is → second conjugation, with a dropped letter.** *Oscail, inis, freagair, imir, codail, labhair.*

Exceptions to learn: *foghlaim* (learn) is second conjugation even though it doesn't end in *-igh* — *foghlaimím, foghlaimíonn tú*. On the other hand, *tiomáin* (drive) looks second conjugation but isn't — it is **first**, because its vowel is long: *tiomáinim*, *tiomáineann tú*.

blocks.text: Watch the "negative" and "question" columns — that is where most of the surprises are.
How to say the most common ones: *deirim* = DYEH-rim, *déanaim* = DYAY-nim, *faighim* = FAI-yim, *feicim* = FEH-kim, *tugaim* = TOO-gim, *tagaim* = TAH-gim, *téim* = TYAYM.

blocks.title: Three traps in this table
items: **The stem and the present form are often far apart.** *Tabhair* → *tugaim*; *tar* → *tagaim*; *téigh* → *téim*; *abair* → *deirim*. To find *tugaim* in a dictionary, look under *tabhair*.
**Ní deirim takes no séimhiú.** *Abair* is the only verb that isn't softened after *ní*. All the others obey: *ní dhéanaim*, *ní thugaim*, *ní théim*.
**Faighim and feicim take bhf- in questions,** not *bf-*: *an bhfaigheann tú?*, *an bhfeiceann tú?* This is ordinary urú on *f*, just like *an bhfuil*.
